summary: Specifies protocols and procedures for forwarding Broadcast, Unknown Unicast, or Multicast (BUM) traffic of Ethernet VPNs using Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER).

plainLanguage.summary: BIER marks which receivers want a message in a single bit string, so the network copies it only where needed. This applies that to virtual networks.

questions: what is evpn bum over bier
what tunnel type does bier use in evpn
how does evpn split horizon work with bier
subtitle: How Ethernet VPNs can carry broadcast, unknown-unicast and multicast traffic over a BIER network core.

tldr.problem: Ethernet VPNs need provider tunnels to carry Broadcast, Unknown Unicast and Multicast (BUM) traffic, and RFC 7432 and RFC 8365 allow several tunnel technologies but do not cover BIER.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reuses the PMSI Tunnel Attribute and much of the MVPN-over-BIER procedure from RFC 8556, with tunnel type 0x0B, an upstream-assigned label or VNI/VSID, and a BIER header whose bit string names the egress PEs.
tldr.outcome: EVPN can use BIER as a provider tunnel without per-flow state in the core, and IANA registered three new BIER next-protocol values and two multicast addresses for it.

today: RFC 9624 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2024. The unit metadata shows that no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 7432 and RFC 8365 define Ethernet VPNs (EVPN). For Broadcast, Unknown Unicast, or Multicast (BUM) traffic they use provider tunnels, and several tunnel technologies are allowed. This document adds one more: Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER) from RFC 8279.

BIER gives optimal multicast forwarding through a multicast domain without making intermediate routers keep per-flow state or run an explicit tree-building protocol.

An EVPN Broadcast Domain (BD) plays the role that a VPN plays in Multicast VPN (MVPN). So this RFC closely follows RFC 8556, which specifies MVPN with BIER, and it borrows some text from it verbatim. Background that RFC 8556 already covers is not repeated.
sections.plainLanguage: Some networks send one message to many people. BIER is a smart way to do that, and this RFC says how virtual Ethernet networks can use it.

sections.title: The PMSI Tunnel Attribute for BIER
sections.content:
An Inclusive Multicast Ethernet Tag (IMET) route carries a PMSI Tunnel Attribute (PTA) that names the provider tunnel for one or more BUM flows. For BIER the PTA is encoded as in RFC 8556, with these fields.

  • Tunnel Type: the same codepoint 0x0B that IANA assigned to BIER for MVPN.
  • Tunnel Identifier: three subfields. The first is a one-octet BIER sub-domain-id. The second is a two-octet BFR-id of the router building the PTA. The third is that router's BFR-Prefix, either a /32 IPv4 address or a /128 IPv6 address.
  • MPLS Label: for EVPN-MPLS, an upstream-assigned label chosen by the ingress router (the BFIR). For EVPN-VXLAN, NVGRE or GENEVE, a 24-bit VNI/VSID of global significance.
  • Flags: two flags matter for BIER, Leaf Info Required per Flow (LIR-pF) and Leaf Info Required (LIR).

A route with a BIER PTA, if it is an IMET, S-PMSI A-D or per-region I-PMSI A-D route, MUST NOT be distributed beyond the boundaries of a BIER domain. Distribution is still controlled by Route Targets.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel announcement is like a label on a delivery truck. It says which delivery system to use, who started it, and which compartment holds which network's parcels.

sections.title: IP-Based Tunnels and BIER PHP
sections.content:
By default, when VXLAN, NVGRE or GENEVE is used for EVPN, the outer IP header (and UDP header for VXLAN and GENEVE) is left out of the BIER payload.

There is one exception. When it is known in advance that BIER Penultimate Hop Popping is used in the BIER domain, and the encapsulation between the penultimate hop and the egress PE cannot say that the next header is VXLAN, NVGRE or GENEVE, the full encapsulation MUST be used. The outer destination address is then the well-known multicast address 224.0.0.122 for IPv4 or FF02:0:0:0:0:0:0:14 for IPv6. Egress PEs MUST be set up to receive it. The same address serves all BDs, and the inner VXLAN, NVGRE or GENEVE header identifies the BD.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the extra outer envelope is left off. If the last helper along the way would not know what is inside, the full envelope goes back on with a shared address.

sections.title: Explicit Tracking and the MPLS Label
sections.content:
An ingress PE acts as a BFIR, so it must know which egress routers (BFERs) need each packet. Two ways are described, both called explicit tracking.

  • IMET and SMET routes: for an inclusive PMSI, the egress set is the originators of all IMET routes for the BD. For a selective PMSI it is the originators of the matching SMET routes. SMET routes carry no PTA, so the ingress PE uses the upstream-assigned label from its own IMET route.
  • S-PMSI and Leaf A-D routes: needed when selective forwarding is used only for some flows, or for tunnel segmentation (EVPN-MPLS only). The rules in sections 2.2.1 and 2.2.2 of RFC 8556 apply, except that section 2.2.2 does not apply to segmentation because the LIR-pF flag cannot be used with segmentation.

For the MPLS label in the PTA, the rules in section 2.1 of RFC 8556 apply with three exceptions. The bullets about differing address families, MVPN extranet VRFs, and the Extranet Separation community do not apply to EVPN.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending, the sender must know who wants a copy. It can learn this from sign-up notes that receivers post, or from replies to a specific invitation.

sections.title: Multihoming Split Horizon
sections.content:
When one customer site connects to several PEs (multihoming), a BUM packet must not be sent back to the Ethernet segment it came from. For EVPN-MPLS, RFC 7432 uses ESI labels. For EVPN-VXLAN, NVGRE and GENEVE, RFC 8365 uses local bias, where the receiving PE knows the ingress PE from the encapsulation.

With BIER both still apply. For local bias, the BFIR-id in the BIER header identifies the ingress PE. For EVPN-MPLS, two upstream-assigned labels are used, one for the BD and one for the Ethernet segment. The BFIR-id identifies the PE that assigned them.
sections.plainLanguage: If you shout news into a room and the person next to you already heard it, nobody should shout it back at them. This rule keeps copies from going back to where they started.

sections.title: Data Plane: Encapsulation and Disposition
sections.content:
EVPN acts as the multicast flow overlay of RFC 8279. At an ingress PE, the packet first gets an upstream-assigned ESI label if it came from a multihomed segment, EVPN-MPLS is in use and ESI labels are used for split horizon. Then the PTA label is pushed for EVPN-MPLS. For VXLAN, NVGRE or GENEVE, the matching header is added with the VNI/VSID from the PTA label field, plus an IP/UDP header if needed.

The packet is then wrapped in a BIER header per RFC 8279 and RFC 8296. The leaf-tracking routes decide which BFERs are set in the header. The route matched for transmission depends on whether selective forwarding applies, using IMET, SMET or S-PMSI A-D routes according to numbered rules. If no route matches, or a tunnel needing leaf tracking has no leaf-tracking routes, the packet is not sent on a P-tunnel.

A BFIR may instead be a P-tunnel segmentation point. It removes the upstream encapsulation, swaps the label to the one in the PTA of the re-advertised route, and imposes a BIER header.

At the egress, the BD is found from the upstream-assigned label or the VNI/VSID, and normal EVPN forwarding follows. With EVPN-MPLS, an inner label after the BIER header is treated as the ESI label for split horizon.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender puts the parcel in the right box, adds a card listing who gets a copy, and hands it to the network. At the far end, the label says which neighborhood the parcel belongs to.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered three values in the "BIER Next Protocol Identifiers" registry: 7 for a VXLAN payload with no IP/UDP header, 8 for NVGRE with no IP header, and 9 for GENEVE with no IP/UDP header.

IANA also assigned a multicast address for the case in section 2.1, described as "Network Virtualization Overlay (NVO) BUM Traffic": 224.0.0.122 in the IPv4 Local Network Control Block and FF02:0:0:0:0:0:0:14 in the IPv6 Link-Local Scope Multicast Addresses registry.
sections.plainLanguage: The number keeper wrote down new codes so everyone uses the same numbers for the same kinds of parcels.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says that using BIER as EVPN provider tunnels is very similar to using it for MVPN. It states that it does not introduce security implications beyond those already discussed in RFC 7432 and RFC 8556.
sections.plainLanguage: This idea does not add new dangers beyond those the older systems already have.
